\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
In ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation, internal reasoning is error-prone---the model may hallucinate state changes (e.g., that water has boiled when the stove was never activated)---while deterministic external computation eliminates such errors via exact state transitions. The practical question: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision: Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} inserts API calls by perplexity reduction; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects heterogeneous modules per subtask; adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}; concurrent analyses further presuppose diverse routing signals~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026}. The shared assumption---that routing signal stems from diverse sources and a learned router can exploit it---has not been tested: no prior work has decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments.

We propose a \emph{diagnostic framework} comprising (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), which decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding. Under ScienceWorld's penalty ($P{=}100$), DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$). The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic death ($-100$ penalty); once death episodes are removed, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$ (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% tie rate; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). Our approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode outcomes.

Cross-context checks probe specificity: MATH Level~4--5 ($N{=}795$, code interpreter) shows no routing signal without catastrophic failure ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$); Llama-3.1-8B replication ($N{=}220$) confirms death dominance across model families (direction consistency 10/10; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}). Four intervention axes (retry, Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023}, $10{\times}$ scaling, action-space restriction) reduce death rates but none closes the gap to deterministic safety, with ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions: (1)~an \textbf{episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} that overcomes per-step oracle degeneracy (97.4\% tie rate) in sparse-reward environments, enabling routing signal decomposition (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}); (2)~applying this framework to ScienceWorld, we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a single mechanism dominates routing signal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); (3)~\textbf{cross-model validation} (Llama-3.1-8B, DAF${=}88.2\%$), four intervention axes, and cross-environment boundary probes (MATH, ALFWorld) confirm the framework's diagnostic utility and the robustness of the finding (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).

lines: All 105 internal-strategy deaths trace to misuse of \texttt{focus on [object]}, the answer-submission action, as a general interaction command (Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}). The root cause is grounding failure: agents parse task descriptions correctly but cannot map understanding to valid primitives. The internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\ 40) reflects more frequent entry into catastrophic states, not different within-episode behavior (${\sim}5\%$ \texttt{focus on} rate in both); lethality depends jointly on misuse rate and answer distribution (\texttt{find-non-living-thing}: zero deaths despite high submission rate). Direct grounding interventions reduce but do not eliminate vulnerability ($48.0\% \to 29.0\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}).
\paragraph{Practical value of routing.}

-The framework reveals that 96.3\% of oracle decisions favor always-deterministic, with 61.2\% of episodes showing no strategy preference---routing is nearly unnecessary on ScienceWorld. This diagnostic finding matters because it prevents wasted computation: a ${\sim}$50-episode pilot (Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}) correctly predicts outcomes for all four conditions, while our router training consumed ${\sim}$200 GPU-hours without exceeding the always-deterministic baseline.

The penalty-independent label fraction (78.9\%) is the primary diagnostic; DAF increases monotonically with $P$ (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}). 6	\emph{Token-level} methods embed tools into the model vocabulary: ToolkenGPT \cite{toolkengpt-2023} represents tools as special tokens resolved at inference.
7	\emph{Task-level} decomposition routes subtasks to specialized modules: ART \cite{art-2023} generates tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} composes heterogeneous modules per subtask.
8	\emph{RL-based} methods learn routing policies from reward: ReTool \cite{retool-2025} discovers when code execution is preferable to chain-of-thought.
9	All focus on \emph{learning to use tools}; we ask a prior question: \emph{what signal drives the routing decision?}
10	Concurrent work examines \emph{when} to invoke tools: \citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} find tool overuse correlates with model uncertainty; \citet{when2tool-2026} show tool-call decisions are encoded in hidden states; \citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax''; \citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity-utility-affordability framework. Our decomposition provides environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of routing labels trace to catastrophic-failure prevention.
11	
12	\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}
13	Adaptive routing traces back to learned halting policies \citep{graves2016act}. In the LLM era, CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels, Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths, and MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing.
14	RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from preference data to select between strong and weak models.
15	These optimize \emph{how} to route; we reveal \emph{why} routing helps: in interactive environments, the dominant signal is catastrophic-failure avoidance.
16	
17	\paragraph{Counterfactual Evaluation in RL.}
18	Prior work generates counterfactual explanations for RL agents by perturbing individual actions within a fixed policy \citep{olson2021counterfactual, gajcin2023counterfactual, amitai2024explaining}.
19	Our approach differs in both purpose and granularity: we execute two complete episodes under different routing strategies, producing prospective paired comparisons that isolate routing signal \emph{before} any router is trained.
20	
21	\paragraph{LLM Agent Environments and Reasoning.}
22	ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} serves as our primary testbed; ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} provides a complementary household environment; AgentBench \cite{agentbench-2024} offers systematic evaluation. \citet{zhou2024webarena} document common failure modes (premature termination, hallucinated actions) in web-based agents, consistent with our finding that state hallucination is the primary failure mechanism. ReAct \cite{react-2023} serves as our internal baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-reflection; LATS \cite{lats-2024} adds tree search.
23	
24	\paragraph{Safe RL.}
25	Death avoidance as an implicit routing signal connects to safe RL. Constrained MDPs \citep{altman1999constrained} formalize safety through state or cost constraints; our mechanism can be viewed as an implicit absorbing-state constraint. Risk-sensitive RL \citep{mihatsch2002risk} optimizes CVaR-type objectives; our framework diagnoses when such risk-sensitivity emerges rather than prescribing it. Classical methods \citep{garcia2015comprehensive,tamar2015cvar,achiam2017cpo,crpo-2021,moldovan2012safe} require explicit constraint specification; our routing achieves safety implicitly through computation mode selection. \citet{ruan2024failures} provide a taxonomy of LM agent failures identifying catastrophic actions as a distinct category, consistent with our finding. SafeRoute \citep{saferoute-2025} applies adaptive model selection for safety guardrails.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
In ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation, internal reasoning is error-prone---the model may hallucinate state changes (e.g., that water has boiled when the stove was never activated)---while deterministic external computation eliminates such errors via exact state transitions. The practical question: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision: Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} inserts API calls by perplexity reduction; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects heterogeneous modules per subtask; adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}; concurrent analyses further presuppose diverse routing signals~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026}. The shared assumption---that routing signal stems from diverse sources and a learned router can exploit it---has not been tested: no prior work has decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments.

We propose a \emph{diagnostic framework} comprising (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), which decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding. Under ScienceWorld's penalty ($P{=}100$), DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$). The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic death ($-100$ penalty); once death episodes are removed, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$ (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% tie rate; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). Our approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode outcomes.

Cross-context checks probe specificity: MATH Level~4--5 ($N{=}795$, code interpreter) shows no routing signal without catastrophic failure ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$); Llama-3.1-8B replication ($N{=}220$) confirms death dominance across model families (direction consistency 10/10; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}). Four intervention axes (retry, Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023}, $10{\times}$ scaling, action-space restriction) reduce death rates but none closes the gap to deterministic safety, with ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions: (1)~an \textbf{episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} that overcomes per-step oracle degeneracy (97.4\% tie rate) and produces three interpretable outputs: penalty-independent label fractions, a Death Avoidance Factor decomposition, and oracle degeneracy detection (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}), enabling practitioners to assess routing value from a ${\sim}$50-episode pilot before investing in router training; (2)~applying this framework to ScienceWorld, we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a single mechanism dominates routing signal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); (3)~\textbf{cross-model validation} (Llama-3.1-8B, DAF${=}88.2\%$), four intervention axes, and cross-environment boundary probes (MATH, ALFWorld) confirm the framework's diagnostic utility and the robustness of the finding (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
In ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation, internal reasoning is error-prone---the model may hallucinate state changes (e.g., that water has boiled when the stove was never activated)---while deterministic external computation eliminates such errors via exact state transitions. The practical question: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision: Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} inserts API calls by perplexity reduction; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects heterogeneous modules per subtask; adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}; concurrent analyses further presuppose diverse routing signals~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026}. The shared assumption---that routing signal stems from diverse sources and a learned router can exploit it---has not been tested: no prior work has decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments.

We propose a \emph{diagnostic framework} comprising (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), which decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding. Under ScienceWorld's penalty ($P{=}100$), DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$). The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic death ($-100$ penalty); once death episodes are removed, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$ (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% tie rate; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). Our approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode outcomes.

Cross-context checks probe specificity: MATH Level~4--5 ($N{=}795$, code interpreter) shows no routing signal without catastrophic failure ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$); Llama-3.1-8B replication ($N{=}220$) confirms death dominance across model families (direction consistency 10/10; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}). Four intervention axes (retry, Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023}, $10{\times}$ scaling, action-space restriction) reduce death rates but none closes the gap to deterministic safety, with ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions: (1)~an \textbf{episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} that overcomes per-step oracle degeneracy (97.4\% tie rate) and produces three interpretable outputs: penalty-independent label fractions, a Death Avoidance Factor decomposition, and oracle degeneracy detection (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}), enabling practitioners to assess routing value from a ${\sim}$50-episode pilot before investing in router training; (2)~applying this framework to ScienceWorld, we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a single mechanism dominates routing signal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); (3)~\textbf{cross-model validation} (Llama-3.1-8B, DAF${=}88.2\%$), four intervention axes, and cross-environment boundary probes (MATH, ALFWorld) confirm the framework's diagnostic utility and the robustness of the finding (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).

lines: \begin{abstract}

-Per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards---in ScienceWorld, 97.4\% of steps yield identical scores regardless of computation mode. We introduce an episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework that overcomes this degeneracy by decomposing routing signal into death-avoidance and non-death components via paired pure-strategy episodes. Applying this framework to ScienceWorld (11 task types, 245 episodes, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent result; a derived measure (DAF) reaches 90.4\% at $P{=}100$. Cross-model replication (Llama-3.1-8B, DAF${=}88.2\%$), four intervention axes (retry, self-correction, $10{\times}$ scaling, action-space restriction), and boundary probes against contrasting environments (MATH, ALFWorld) confirm the framework's diagnostic utility and the robustness of this finding. The framework diagnoses when catastrophic failure makes routing signal degenerate, enabling practitioners to assess routing value before investing in router training.

Applying this framework to ScienceWorld (11 task types, 245 episodes, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent result; a derived measure (DAF) reaches 90.4\% at $P{=}100$. A three-stage diagnostic pilot (${\sim}$50 episodes) correctly predicts routing outcomes across all four tested conditions, demonstrating practical utility before any router is trained.

However, the complete collapse to majority-class prediction (internal recall $= 0.0$) occurs even at the smallest unaugmented scale (25\%, ${\sim}90\%$ det); this is not an augmentation artifact. \paragraph{Per-task-type evaluation breakdown.} To test whether the router learns transferable routing strategies or merely task-type classification, we evaluate existing checkpoints (8 seeds) separately on each of the 11 task types. \section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
In ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation, internal reasoning is error-prone---the model may hallucinate state changes (e.g., that water has boiled when the stove was never activated)---while deterministic external computation eliminates such errors via exact state transitions. The practical question: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision: Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} inserts API calls by perplexity reduction; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects heterogeneous modules per subtask; adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}; concurrent analyses further presuppose diverse routing signals~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026}. The shared assumption---that routing signal stems from diverse sources and a learned router can exploit it---has not been tested: no prior work has decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments.

We propose a \emph{diagnostic framework} comprising (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), which decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding. Under ScienceWorld's penalty ($P{=}100$), DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$). The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic death ($-100$ penalty); once death episodes are removed, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$ (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% tie rate; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). Our approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode outcomes.

Cross-context checks probe specificity: MATH Level~4--5 ($N{=}795$, code interpreter) shows no routing signal without catastrophic failure ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$); Llama-3.1-8B replication ($N{=}220$) confirms death dominance across model families (direction consistency 10/10; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}). Four intervention axes (retry, Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023}, $10{\times}$ scaling, action-space restriction) reduce death rates but none closes the gap to deterministic safety, with ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions: (1)~an \textbf{episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} that overcomes per-step oracle degeneracy (97.4\% tie rate), decomposes routing signal via penalty-independent (label fraction) and penalty-dependent (DAF) metrics, and predicts routing value from a ${\sim}$50-episode pilot (validated 4/4 conditions; Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}); (2)~applying this framework to ScienceWorld, we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a single mechanism that persists across four intervention axes and three model scales, contradicting the routing literature's implicit assumption of diverse signal sources (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); (3)~\textbf{cross-model validation} (Llama-3.1-8B, DAF${=}88.2\%$), four intervention axes, and cross-environment boundary probes (MATH, ALFWorld) confirm the framework's diagnostic utility and the robustness of the finding (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).
